questions.question: List out the properties of food additives.
questions.solution_html:
• List out the properties of food additives.
  • Preservation
  • • Preservation is one of the most important functions of food additives. Preservatives
  • extend the shelf life of foods by inhibiting the growth of spoilage and microorganisms
  • such as bacteria, yeasts and molds. Eg: potassium sorbate and sodium benzoate are
  • commonly used in beverages, sauces, pickles and bakery products to inhibit molds
  • and yeasts.
  • • In addition to microbial control, oxidation (fat react with oxygen to form off-flavour
  • amnd off-odour) is another major cause of food spoilage.
  • Antioxidants such as ascorbic acid (vitamin C) prevent oxidation of fats and oils.
  • Sensory Enhancement
  • • Taste enhancement: Flavouring agents and acids improve palatability (how tasty food
  • is). Monosodium glutamate (MSG) is a flavour enhancer that intensifies umami taste
  • in soups, sauces and processed foods
  • • Appearance : Colour additives restore or enhance the natural colour lost
  • during processing. Natural colours such as carotenoids, annatto, and chlorophyll.
  • • Texture modification: Emulsifiers like lecithin and mono- and diglycerides help in
  • uniform mixing of oil and water in products such as mayonnaise and margarine.
  • Thickeners and stabilizers such as pectin, guar gum and carrageenan improve
  • viscosity, mouthfeel and consistency in sauces, jams and ice cream.
  • • Aroma enhancement: Flavouring substances contribute characteristic aromas, for
  • example vanilla in bakery products or fruit esters in beverages. (smell)
  • Nutritional Enhancement
  • • Food additives play an important role in improving the nutritional quality of foods
  • through fortification. Vitamins such as vitamin A, D and B-complex are added to
  • milk, flour and cereals to prevent deficiency diseases. Minerals like iron, calcium and
  • iodine are incorporated into salt, flour and beverages
  • Processing Aids
  • • Leavening agents, such as baking powder and baking soda, release carbon dioxide
  • during baking, causing dough expansion and producing soft, porous bakery products.
  • • Anti-caking agents like silicon dioxide and calcium silicate prevent clumping in
  • powdered foods such as salt, sugar and spice mixes.
  • • Enzymes used in food processing also fall under processing aids, improving
  • efficiency and product quality. (ptns that speed up chemical reactions)
  • Safety and Stability
  • • Food additives must be safe for human consumption and stable under processing and
  • storage conditions.
  • • Stability ensures that additives do not break down into harmful substances when
  • exposed to heat, light or oxygen.
questions.final_answer: Option (c) prevent oxidation of fats and oils.

questions.question: Explain the concept of intelligent packaging and describe the different types of indicators used in it.
questions.solution_html:
• indicators used in it.
  • Intelligent packaging is defined as packaging that contains an external or internal indicator to
  • provide information about aspects of the history of the package and/or the quality of the food.
  • External indicators are those indicators which are attached outside the package like time
  • temperature indicators
  • Internal indicators are those indicators which are placed inside the package, either to the head
  • space of the package or attached into the lid like oxygen indicators for indication of oxygen or
  • package leak, carbon dioxide indicators, microbial growth indicators and pathogen indicators
  • Various examples of internal and external indicators are shown in the table below
  • Time–Temperature Indicators (TTIs)
  • Time–Temperature Indicators record the temperature history of packaged foods during storage
  • transport, and sale. They provide information about food quality and safety through irreversible
  • changes. TTIs are classified into diffusion, microbial, enzyme, polymerization, and light color
  • types. They are mainly used for temperature-sensitive foods such as frozen and chilled foods.
  • Freshness Indicators
  • Freshness indicators show the freshness of food by detecting metabolites produced during
  • spoilage. These indicators often produce visible color changes when reacting with compounds
  • such as glucose, organic acids, ethanol, volatile nitrogen compounds, CO₂, sulfides, and
  • biogenic amines. They are commonly used for fresh foods like fruits and seafood.
  • Leak Indicators
  • Leak indicators detect changes in gas composition inside food packages caused by respiration
  • microbial activity, or package leakage. They help monitor food quality and safety. Common
  • gases detected include oxygen (O₂) and carbon dioxide (CO₂), while others like water vapor
  • ethanol, and hydrogen sulfide may also be monitored.
  • pH Indicators
  • pH indicators detect changes in pH levels of packaged foods. Natural compounds such as
  • anthocyanins (polyphenols) are commonly used because they change color with pH variations
  • indicating food spoilage.

  • • Texture modification: Emulsifiers like lecithin and mono- and diglycerides help in
  • uniform mixing of oil and water in products such as mayonnaise and margarine.
  • Thickeners and stabilizers such as pectin, guar gum and carrageenan improve
  • viscosity, mouthfeel and consistency in sauces, jams and ice cream.
  • • Aroma enhancement: Flavouring substances contribute characteristic aromas, for
  • example vanilla in bakery products or fruit esters in beverages. (smell)
  • Nutritional Enhancement
  • • Food additives play an important role in improving the nutritional quality of foods
  • through fortification. Vitamins such as vitamin A, D and B-complex are added to
  • milk, flour and cereals to prevent deficiency diseases. Minerals like iron, calcium and
  • iodine are incorporated into salt, flour and beverages
  • Processing Aids
  • • Leavening agents, such as baking powder and baking soda, release carbon dioxide
  • during baking, causing dough expansion and producing soft, porous bakery products.
  • • Anti-caking agents like silicon dioxide and calcium silicate prevent clumping in
  • powdered foods such as salt, sugar and spice mixes.
  • • Enzymes used in food processing also fall under processing aids, improving
  • efficiency and product quality. (ptns that speed up chemical reactions)
  • Safety and Stability
  • • Food additives must be safe for human consumption and stable under processing and
  • storage conditions.
  • • Stability ensures that additives do not break down into harmful substances when
  • exposed to heat, light or oxygen.
questions.final_answer: Option (c) prevent oxidation of fats and oils.

questions.question: Define thickening agents in detail along with its types and functions in food.
questions.solution_html:
• A thickening agent is something you add to a liquid to make it thicker without really changing
  • its taste. In cooking, thickeners are often used to make sauces, soups, and puddings thicker and
  • smoother. They work because their tiny molecules spread out in the liquid and get mixed
  • together. This makes the liquid flow more slowly, so it feels thicker.

  • organisms, or of masking the evidence of any such deterioration.
  • Class I preservatives are natural substances and can be used without restriction e.g. salt
  • sugar, spices, vinegar.
  • Sodium chloride : Salts stop the growth of microorganisms and interfere with the action
  • of proteolytic enzymes. Salts also cause food dehydration by drawing out water from the
  • tissue cells. Used in butter, cheese, cabbage, olives, cucumbers, meat, fish and bread.

  • pressure of sugar creates conditions that are unfavourable for the growth and reproduction
  • of most species of bacteria, yeasts and molds. Used in syrups and confectionary products
  • fondant fillings in chocolate, honey, jellies, marmalades, conserves and fruits such as
  • dates, sultanas and currants.

questions.question: Explain the concept of intelligent packaging and describe the different types of indicators used in it.
questions.solution_html:
• indicators used in it.
  • Intelligent packaging is defined as packaging that contains an external or internal indicator to
  • provide information about aspects of the history of the package and/or the quality of the food.
  • External indicators are those indicators which are attached outside the package like time
  • temperature indicators
  • Internal indicators are those indicators which are placed inside the package, either to the head
  • space of the package or attached into the lid like oxygen indicators for indication of oxygen or
  • package leak, carbon dioxide indicators, microbial growth indicators and pathogen indicators
  • Various examples of internal and external indicators are shown in the table below
  • Time–Temperature Indicators (TTIs)
  • Time–Temperature Indicators record the temperature history of packaged foods during storage
  • transport, and sale. They provide information about food quality and safety through irreversible
  • changes. TTIs are classified into diffusion, microbial, enzyme, polymerization, and light color
  • types. They are mainly used for temperature-sensitive foods such as frozen and chilled foods.
  • Freshness Indicators
  • Freshness indicators show the freshness of food by detecting metabolites produced during
  • spoilage. These indicators often produce visible color changes when reacting with compounds
  • such as glucose, organic acids, ethanol, volatile nitrogen compounds, CO₂, sulfides, and
  • biogenic amines. They are commonly used for fresh foods like fruits and seafood.
  • Leak Indicators
  • Leak indicators detect changes in gas composition inside food packages caused by respiration
  • microbial activity, or package leakage. They help monitor food quality and safety. Common
  • gases detected include oxygen (O₂) and carbon dioxide (CO₂), while others like water vapor
  • ethanol, and hydrogen sulfide may also be monitored.
  • pH Indicators
  • pH indicators detect changes in pH levels of packaged foods. Natural compounds such as
  • anthocyanins (polyphenols) are commonly used because they change color with pH variations
  • indicating food spoilage.
